title: Patching a Cloud Fleet with AWS Systems Manager
intro: In the cloud, fleet patching is often done with the provider's own tooling: AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager (Azure has Update Manager; GCP has VM Manager OS patch management). It scans against a patch baseline, installs in controlled batches, and reports compliance, with no SSH and no Ansible control node.

steps.prompt: Check the patch state of instance i-0a1b2c3d4e5f67890.
steps.fake_output:
InstanceId            PatchGroup  Installed  Missing  Failed  InstalledPendingReboot  OperationEndTime
i-0a1b2c3d4e5f67890   web-prod    412        7        0       2                       2026-09-21T03:10:44Z
steps.explanation: 7 patches missing; 2 installed but waiting for a reboot.
steps.why: 'InstalledPendingReboot' is the Linux-kernel problem again: installed doesn't mean active. Compliance dashboards should count those as not done.

steps.prompt: List which patches are missing on i-0a1b2c3d4e5f67890.
steps.fake_output:
Title                               Severity   State    
openssl-3.0.8-1.amzn2023.0.14       Important  Missing
kernel-6.1.109-118.189.amzn2023     Critical   Missing
curl-8.5.0-1.amzn2023.0.4           Medium     Missing
steps.explanation: A critical kernel patch among them.
steps.why: Patch baselines decide what counts as 'approved' (for example security patches of Critical/Important severity, auto-approved 7 days after release). That delay is deliberate: it lets the wider world discover bad patches before your fleet installs them.

steps.prompt: Scan (don't install) all instances in patch group web-prod.
expected_commands: aws ssm send-command --document-name AWS-RunPatchBaseline --targets Key=tag:PatchGroup,Values=web-prod --parameters Operation=Scan
steps.why: Scan and install are separate operations. Scanning is safe any time and feeds compliance reports; installs happen in maintenance windows.

steps.prompt: Install on web-prod in controlled batches: at most 10% of instances at a time, stopping after 1 error.
expected_commands: aws ssm send-command --document-name AWS-RunPatchBaseline --targets Key=tag:PatchGroup,Values=web-prod --parameters Operation=Install --max-concurrency 10% --max-errors 1
steps.explanation: Patching runs about 3 instances at a time and halts at the first failure.
steps.why: --max-concurrency and --max-errors are SSM's equivalents of Ansible's serial and max_fail_percentage (servers-tutorial-003). Without them, all 24 instances patch and reboot at once. For zero-downtime patching of an Auto Scaling group, prefer replacing instances from a patched AMI (an instance refresh) over patching in place.

steps.prompt: Check results per instance for command 8a7b6c5d-4e3f-4a2b-9c1d-0e9f8a7b6c5d.
steps.fake_output:
InstanceId            Status     
i-0a1b2c3d4e5f67890   Success
i-0b2c3d4e5f6789012   Success
i-0c3d4e5f678901234   Failed    (Error: yum lock held by another process)
(21 instances: not started, because max-errors 1 was reached)
steps.explanation: One failure stopped the rollout; 21 instances untouched.
steps.why: A package-manager lock usually means another update (for example dnf-automatic) was running at the same moment. Don't run two patching mechanisms on the same fleet, because they collide. Fix the cause, then resume.
